content: 1. Epithelial cells from the endocervix or urethra are the primary targets for specimen collection in screening tests. 2. The endocervix is the preferred anatomical site for collecting screening specimens from women. 3. When culture isolation is used, processing an additional specimen from the urethra can increase sensitivity by approximately 23%. 4. It is acceptable to place both endocervical and urethral specimens in the same transport container. 5. For non-culture tests, the utility of a second specimen from the urethra has not been established. 6. The urethra is the preferred site for collecting screening specimens from men. Guidelines for Collecting Endocervical Specimens: 7. Specimens for chlamydia testing should be obtained after collecting specimens for Gram-stained smear, Neisseria gonorrhoeae culture, or Papanicolaou smear. 8. Before obtaining a specimen for chlamydia testing, use a sponge or large swab to remove all secretions and discharge from the cervical os. 9. For non-culture chlamydia tests, use the swab provided or specified by the test manufacturer. 10. Insert the appropriate swab or endocervical brush 1-2 cm into the endocervical canal, past the squamocolumnar junction. 11. Rotate the swab against the wall of the endocervical canal several times for 10-30 seconds. 12. Withdraw the swab without touching any vaginal surfaces and place it in the appropriate transport medium (culture, EIA, or DNA probe testing) or prepare a slide for direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing. Guidelines for Collecting Urethral Specimens: 13. Delay specimen collection until at least 2 hours after the patient has voided. 14. Obtain specimens for chlamydia testing after collecting specimens for Gram-stain smear or Neisseria gonorrhoeae culture. 15. For non-culture chlamydia tests, use the swab provided or specified by the test manufacturer. 16. Gently insert the urogenital swab into the urethra (1-2 cm for females, 2-4 cm for males). 17. Rotate the swab in one direction for at least one full revolution over 5 seconds. 18. Withdraw the swab and place it in the appropriate transport medium (culture, EIA, or DNA probe testing) or use it to prepare a slide for DFA testing. Quality Assurance of Specimen Collection: 19. Without quality assurance, at least 10% of specimens may be unsatisfactory due to the presence of secretions or exudate but lack of urethral or endocervical columnar cells. 20. Cell Culture for Chlamydia Detection: 21. A major advantage of cell culture isolation is its specificity, which approaches 100%. 22. In cell culture, organisms from all three chlamydia species (C. trachomatis, C. pneumoniae, and C. psittaci) grow and produce characteristic intracellular inclusions. 23. Direct visualization of these inclusions contributes to the specificity of cell culture in identifying chlamydia. 24. The preferred method for identifying inclusions is staining infected cells with a species-specific, monoclonal fluorescein-labeled antibody (FA) for C. trachomatis. 25. Antibodies that bind to chlamydia lipopolysaccharide (LPS) are not specific for C. trachomatis and may also stain inclusions from C. psittaci and C. pneumoniae. 26. The use of C. trachomatis-specific anti-major outer membrane protein (MOMP) antibody is presumed to be the method for detecting C. trachomatis in cell culture. 27. Culture sensitivity ranges from 70% to 90% in experienced laboratories. 28. Cell culture is preferred for specimens with low numbers of organisms, such as those from asymptomatic infections. 29. Culture allows the organism to be preserved for additional studies, including serovar determination and antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Disadvantages of Cell Culture: 30. Cell culture is technically challenging and requires 3-7 days to obtain results. 31. Only viable organisms are detected, necessitating the use of special transport media and strict temperature requirements during transportation and storage. 32. Some specimens may contain contaminating microorganisms or substances toxic to the cell monolayers used for isolating chlamydia. Indications for the Use of Cell Culture: 33. A high-quality culture system is the diagnostic method of choice for chlamydia in all medical or legal situations. 34. Culture serves as the standard for quality assurance of non-culture tests and for evaluating new diagnostic methods. 35. Culture is recommended for detecting chlamydia in specimens where non-culture methods are unavailable, inadequately evaluated, or perform poorly. 36. Culture is recommended for specimens from the following sites: Urethral specimens (women and asymptomatic men) Nasopharyngeal specimens (infants) Rectal specimens (all patients, regardless of age) Vaginal specimens (prepubertal girls) Collecting Specimens for Cell Culture: 37. Swabs with plastic or wire shafts can be used to obtain cell cultures. 38. Swab tips may be made of cotton, rayon, Dacron, or calcium alginate. 39. Swabs with wooden shafts should not be used, as wood may contain substances toxic to chlamydia. 40. Routine quality control should include screening each lot of swabs for potential toxicity to chlamydia. 41. Substituting an endocervical brush for a swab may increase the sensitivity of culture for endocervical specimens from nonpregnant women. 42. However, the use of an endocervical brush may induce bleeding, which does not interfere with the isolation of C. trachomatis but may cause spotting. Transporting Cell Culture Specimens: 43. The viability of chlamydia organisms must be maintained during transport to the laboratory. 44. Consult the laboratory regarding the selection of appropriate transport medium and procedures. 45. Specimens for culture should be stored at 4°C and inoculated in cell culture as quickly as possible, ideally within 24 hours. 46. If inoculation cannot occur within 24 hours, specimens should be maintained at -70°C or colder. 47. Specimens should never be stored at -20°C or in frost-free freezers, as these conditions reduce chlamydia viability. 48. Only cell lines verified for their ability to support chlamydial growth should be used. Analyzing Cell Culture Specimens: 49. Identification of C. trachomatis should be based on visualizing characteristic chlamydia inclusions using species-specific FA staining. 50. Laboratories should periodically assess whether multiple passages increase sensitivity. Interpreting Cell Culture Results: 51. A positive cell culture and visualization of characteristic inclusions by species-specific monoclonal FA staining are required to diagnose a chlamydial infection. 52. The specificity of culture is based on the identification of inclusions. 53. Identification of chlamydia after culture by EIA or other methods that do not identify characteristic inclusions is not recommended.
